claim: DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair by homologous recombination is confined to the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle partly due to 53BP1 antagonizing DNA end resection in G1 phase and non-cycling quiescent (G0) cells.
source: DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair by homologous recombination is confined to the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle partly due to 53BP1 antagonizing DNA end resection in G1 phase and non-cycling quiescent (G0) cells where DSBs are predominately repaired by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: DSBs in G0 cells are predominately repaired by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
source: DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair by homologous recombination is confined to the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle partly due to 53BP1 antagonizing DNA end resection in G1 phase and non-cycling quiescent (G0) cells where DSBs are predominately repaired by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: Extensive MRE11- and CtIP-dependent DNA end resection occurs at DSBs in G0 murine and human cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we uncovered extensive MRE11- and CtIP-dependent DNA end resection at DSBs in G0 murine and human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1C.

claim: A whole genome CRISPR/Cas9 screen revealed the DNA-dependent kinase (DNA-PK) complex as a key factor in promoting DNA end resection in G0 cells.
source: A whole genome CRISPR/Cas9 screen revealed the DNA-dependent kinase (DNA-PK) complex as a key factor in promoting DNA end resection in G0 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Depletion of FBXL12 promotes more extensive resection in G0 cells.
source: In agreement, depletion of FBXL12, which promotes ubiquitylation and removal of the KU70/KU80 subunits of DNA-PK from DSBs, promotes even more extensive resection in G0 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FBXL12 promotes ubiquitylation and removal of the KU70/KU80 subunits of DNA-PK from DSBs.
source: In agreement, depletion of FBXL12, which promotes ubiquitylation and removal of the KU70/KU80 subunits of DNA-PK from DSBs, promotes even more extensive resection in G0 cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the discussion section.

claim: A requirement for DNA-PK in promoting DNA end resection in proliferating cells at the G1 or G2 phase of the cell cycle was not observed.
source: In contrast, a requirement for DNA-PK in promoting DNA end resection in proliferating cells at the G1 or G2 phase of the cell cycle was not observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DNA-PK uniquely promotes DNA end resection in G0, but not in G1 or G2 phase cells.
source: Our findings establish that DNA-PK uniquely promotes DNA end resection in G0, but not in G1 or G2 phase cells, which has important implications for DNA DSB repair in quiescent cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) can lead to cell death if left unrepaired.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are particularly deleterious lesions which, if left unrepaired, can lead to cell death, or if repaired aberrantly, can lead to oncogenic chromosomal translocations and deletions (Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jackson and Bartek, 2009.

claim: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) can lead to oncogenic chromosomal translocations and deletions if repaired aberrantly.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are particularly deleterious lesions which, if left unrepaired, can lead to cell death, or if repaired aberrantly, can lead to oncogenic chromosomal translocations and deletions (Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jackson and Bartek, 2009.

claim: Eukaryotic cells utilize two main mechanisms of DSB repair: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR).
source: Eukaryotic cells utilize two main mechanisms of DSB repair: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), where the broken DNA ends are ligated together with minimal processing of the DNA termini; and homologous recombination (HR), which uses a homologous sequence, usually on a sister chromatid, as a template for accurate DNA repair.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: In NHEJ, broken DNA ends are ligated together with minimal processing of the DNA termini.
source: Eukaryotic cells utilize two main mechanisms of DSB repair: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), where the broken DNA ends are ligated together with minimal processing of the DNA termini; and homologous recombination (HR), which uses a homologous sequence, usually on a sister chromatid, as a template for accurate DNA repair.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: Homologous recombination (HR) uses a homologous sequence, usually on a sister chromatid, as a template for accurate DNA repair.
source: Eukaryotic cells utilize two main mechanisms of DSB repair: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), where the broken DNA ends are ligated together with minimal processing of the DNA termini; and homologous recombination (HR), which uses a homologous sequence, usually on a sister chromatid, as a template for accurate DNA repair.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: HR is mostly restricted to S and G2 phases of the cell cycle when sister chromatids exist.
source: Because HR relies on a homologous template for accurate repair, HR is mostly restricted to S and G2 phases of the cell cycle when sister chromatids exist.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: Cells can employ NHEJ in any phase of the cell cycle.
source: On the other hand, cells can employ NHEJ in any phase of the cell cycle and it is the only option in quiescent (G0) cells and G1 phase cells (Scully et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Scully et al., 2019.

claim: NHEJ is the only DSB repair option in quiescent (G0) cells and G1 phase cells.
source: On the other hand, cells can employ NHEJ in any phase of the cell cycle and it is the only option in quiescent (G0) cells and G1 phase cells (Scully et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Scully et al., 2019.

claim: Extensive DNA end resection of the broken DNA ends generates long tracts of 3' ssDNA overhangs at DSBs.
source: Extensive DNA end resection of the broken DNA ends, which generates long tracts of 3' ssDNA overhangs at DSBs, is a critical step in committing the cell to use HR to repair DSBs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: Extensive DNA end resection is a critical step in committing the cell to use HR to repair DSBs.
source: Extensive DNA end resection of the broken DNA ends, which generates long tracts of 3' ssDNA overhangs at DSBs, is a critical step in committing the cell to use HR to repair DSBs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: DNA end resection is initiated by nucleases MRE11 and CtIP.
source: DNA end resection is initiated by nucleases MRE11 and CtIP, and subsequently extended by nucleases including EXO1 and DNA2/BLM (Paull and Gellert, 1998; Trujillo et al., 1998; Sartori et al., 2007; Gravel et al., 2008; Mimitou and Symington, 2008; Zhu et al., 2008; Bunting et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: DNA end resection is subsequently extended by nucleases including EXO1 and DNA2/BLM.
source: DNA end resection is initiated by nucleases MRE11 and CtIP, and subsequently extended by nucleases including EXO1 and DNA2/BLM (Paull and Gellert, 1998; Trujillo et al., 1998; Sartori et al., 2007; Gravel et al., 2008; Mimitou and Symington, 2008; Zhu et al., 2008; Bunting et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The 3' ssDNA overhangs are quickly bound by the single-stranded binding protein trimer replication protein A (RPA) to stabilize and protect the ssDNA.
source: The 3' ssDNA overhangs are quickly bound by the single-stranded binding protein trimer replication protein A (RPA) to stabilize and protect the ssDNA, and later in repair RPA is replaced by the RAD51 recombinase protein that leads to the homology search to find a homologous template to achieve accurate HR repair (Sugiyama and Kowalczykowski, 2002; San Filippo et al., 2008; Wright et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RPA is replaced by the RAD51 recombinase protein that leads to the homology search to find a homologous template to achieve accurate HR repair.
source: The 3' ssDNA overhangs are quickly bound by the single-stranded binding protein trimer replication protein A (RPA) to stabilize and protect the ssDNA, and later in repair RPA is replaced by the RAD51 recombinase protein that leads to the homology search to find a homologous template to achieve accurate HR repair (Sugiyama and Kowalczykowski, 2002; San Filippo et al., 2008; Wright et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NHEJ is initiated by the KU70/KU80 heterodimer binding to broken DNA ends.
source: NHEJ is initiated by the KU70/KU80 heterodimer binding to broken DNA ends (Zahid et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Zahid et al., 2021.

claim: KU70/KU80 recruits the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs) which together form a complex called DNA-PK.
source: KU70/KU80 recruits the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs) which together form a complex called DNA-PK (Gottlieb and Jackson, 1993; Hammarsten and Chu, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Once the DNA-PK complex is formed, the KU heterodimer translocates inwards along the DNA and DNA-PKcs remains at the DNA ends.
source: Once the DNA-PK complex is formed, the KU heterodimer translocates inwards along the DNA and DNA-PKcs remains at the DNA ends, undergoing activation via conformational changes mediated by autophosphorylation of the ABCDE cluster (Yaneva et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DNA-PKcs undergoes activation via conformational changes mediated by autophosphorylation of the ABCDE cluster.
source: Once the DNA-PK complex is formed, the KU heterodimer translocates inwards along the DNA and DNA-PKcs remains at the DNA ends, undergoing activation via conformational changes mediated by autophosphorylation of the ABCDE cluster (Yaneva et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of DNA-PK implicate dimerization of DNA-PK as important in recruiting downstream NHEJ factors by bringing broken DNA ends together.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures of DNA-PK also implicate dimerization of DNA-PK as important in recruiting downstream NHEJ factors by bringing broken DNA ends together (Chaplin et al., 2021; Zha et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Chaplin et al., 2021 and Zha et al., 2021.

claim: DNA-PKcs phosphorylates members of the NHEJ machinery, including the KU heterodimer, XRCC4, XLF, and Artemis.
source: In addition to autophosphorylation, DNA-PKcs phosphorylates members of the NHEJ machinery, including the KU heterodimer, XRCC4, XLF, and Artemis (Bartlett and Lees-Miller, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bartlett and Lees-Miller, 2018.

claim: The critical bifurcation point in the choice to use HR or NHEJ to repair DSBs is the processing of broken DNA ends to form single-stranded 3' DNA overhangs.
source: The critical bifurcation point in the choice to use HR or NHEJ to repair DSBs is the processing of broken DNA ends to form single-stranded 3' DNA overhangs, which blocks NHEJ and commits the cell to HR (Symington and Gautier, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Symington and Gautier, 2011.

claim: Processing of broken DNA ends to form single-stranded 3' DNA overhangs blocks NHEJ and commits the cell to HR.
source: The critical bifurcation point in the choice to use HR or NHEJ to repair DSBs is the processing of broken DNA ends to form single-stranded 3' DNA overhangs, which blocks NHEJ and commits the cell to HR (Symington and Gautier, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Symington and Gautier, 2011.

claim: DNA end resection is tightly regulated to prevent aberrant DNA end resection in G0 and G1 phase cells, where NHEJ is the major DSB repair pathway.
source: Therefore, DNA end resection is tightly regulated to prevent aberrant DNA end resection in G0 and G1 phase cells, where NHEJ is the major DSB repair pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: 53BP1, RIF1, and the Shieldin complex are critical DNA end protection factors that limit resection of DNA DSBs.
source: Several factors have been identified as critical DNA end protection factors that limit resection of DNA DSBs including 53BP1, RIF1, and the Shieldin complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: The proposed mechanism of action of 53BP1 and its downstream effectors include acting as a physical barrier to protect DNA ends from nucleases and promoting DNA polymerase α activity to quickly fill in any resected ends.
source: The proposed mechanism of action of 53BP1 and its downstream effectors include acting as a physical barrier to protect DNA ends from nucleases and promoting DNA polymerase α activity to quickly fill in any resected ends (Bunting et al., 2010; Dev et al., 2018; Mirman et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Setiaputra and Durocher, 2019; Paiano et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: KU70/KU80 has been shown in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to inhibit DNA end resection in G1 and G2 phases of the cell cycle.
source: Additionally, KU70/KU80 has also been shown in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to inhibit DNA end resection in G1 and G2 phases of the cell cycle, and in S phase in mammalian cells (Lee et al., 1998; Barlow et al., 2008; Clerici et al., 2008; Shao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: KU70/KU80 has been shown to inhibit DNA end resection in S phase in mammalian cells.
source: Additionally, KU70/KU80 has also been shown in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to inhibit DNA end resection in G1 and G2 phases of the cell cycle, and in S phase in mammalian cells (Lee et al., 1998; Barlow et al., 2008; Clerici et al., 2008; Shao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Artemis is required to open hairpin-sealed DNA ends generated during V(D)J recombination in lymphocytes.
source: For example, Artemis is required to open hairpin-sealed DNA ends generated during V(D)J recombination in lymphocytes (Menon and Povirk, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Menon and Povirk, 2016.

claim: DNA end resection has been observed in G1 phase after DNA damage at complex DNA lesions.
source: Additionally, DNA end resection has been observed in G1 phase after DNA damage at complex DNA lesions (Averbeck et al., 2014; Biehs et al., 2017), suggesting that DNA end resection is not completely inhibited in the absence of sister chromatids.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Averbeck et al., 2014 and Biehs et al., 2017.

claim: CtIP phosphorylation by CDKs in G2 is required for its activity during HR.
source: Moreover, though CtIP phosphorylation by CDKs in G2 is required for its activity during HR, CtIP also functions in G1 at DSBs after phosphorylation by PLK3 (Barton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Barton et al., 2014.

claim: CtIP functions in G1 at DSBs after phosphorylation by PLK3.
source: Moreover, though CtIP phosphorylation by CDKs in G2 is required for its activity during HR, CtIP also functions in G1 at DSBs after phosphorylation by PLK3 (Barton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Barton et al., 2014.

claim: Murine pre-B cells transformed with Abelson murine leukemia virus continuously proliferate in vitro.
source: Murine pre-B cells transformed with Abelson murine leukemia virus (termed abl pre-B cells hereafter) continuously proliferate in vitro and can be efficiently arrested in G0, also referred to as the quiescent state, upon treatment with the abl kinase inhibitor imatinib (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). (Bredemeyer et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Bredemeyer et al., 2006 and Chen et al., 2021a.

claim: Murine abl pre-B cells can be efficiently arrested in G0 upon treatment with the abl kinase inhibitor imatinib.
source: Murine pre-B cells transformed with Abelson murine leukemia virus (termed abl pre-B cells hereafter) continuously proliferate in vitro and can be efficiently arrested in G0, also referred to as the quiescent state, upon treatment with the abl kinase inhibitor imatinib (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). (Bredemeyer et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A high level of chromatin-bound RPA was detected in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Trp53bp1-/- abl pre-B cells after IR.
source: In agreement with our previous work, we detected a high level of chromatin-bound RPA in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Trp53bp1-/- abl pre-B cells after IR, consistent with the role of 53BP1 in DNA end protection (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RPA was observed associated with chromatin after IR of G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells, although at lower levels than in Lig4-/-:Trp53bp1-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: Surprisingly, we also observed RPA associated with chromatin after IR of G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells, although at lower levels than in Lig4-/-:Trp53bp1-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA does not require DNA Ligase IV deficiency.
source: Moreover, the increase in IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA does not require DNA Ligase IV deficiency as we were able to observe similar results using the RPA flow cytometric assay in wild-type (WT) murine abl pre-B cells arrested in G0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Extensive DNA end resection occurs at DSBs in G0 cells, despite the presence of the DNA end protection proteins 53BP1 and KU70/KU80.
source: These data indicate that extensive DNA end resection occurs at DSBs in G0 cells, despite the presence of the DNA end protection proteins 53BP1 and KU70/KU80.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RPA data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of CtIP reduced the levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: We found that the depletion of CtIP or MRE11 reduced the levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the RPA we observe with our flow cytometric assay after IR is indeed a result of DNA end resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Depletion of MRE11 reduced the levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: We found that the depletion of CtIP or MRE11 reduced the levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the RPA we observe with our flow cytometric assay after IR is indeed a result of DNA end resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The RPA observed with flow cytometric assay after IR is a result of DNA end resection.
source: We found that the depletion of CtIP or MRE11 reduced the levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the RPA we observe with our flow cytometric assay after IR is indeed a result of DNA end resection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that depletion of resection nucleases reduces RPA levels.

claim: Artemis depletion had no effect on levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested wildtype abl pre-B cells.
source: We found that Artemis depletion had no effect on levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested wildtype abl pre-B cells, indicating that Artemis activity does not contribute to this process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Artemis activity does not contribute to DNA end resection in G0 cells.
source: We found that Artemis depletion had no effect on levels of RPA on chromatin in irradiated G0-arrested wildtype abl pre-B cells, indicating that Artemis activity does not contribute to this process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no effect of Artemis depletion on RPA levels.

claim: IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA was observed in G0 human MCF10A cells.
source: Similarly, to Lig4-/- and WT murine abl pre-B cells in G0, we observed IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA in G0 human MCF10A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), consistent with DNA end resection occurring in these cells at DSBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Discrete IR-induced RPA foci were observed in EGF-deprived MCF10A cells.
source: Therefore, we performed immunofluorescence staining for RPA in EGF-deprived MCF10A cells. We observed discrete IR-induced RPA foci, consistent with the RPA associated with ssDNA accumulating at DNA damage sites (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Broken DNA ends are resected in a CtIP and MRE11-dependent manner, leading to RPA accumulation on ssDNA in G0 murine and human cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that broken DNA ends are resected in a CtIP and MRE11-dependent manner, leading to RPA accumulation on ssDNA in G0 murine and human cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, 1D, 1E.

claim: RPA binding was detected adjacent to AsiSI DSBs in G0-arrested Lig4-/- murine abl pre-B cells.
source: We detected RPA binding adjacent to AsiSI DSBs, consistent with ssDNA generated by resection around DNA DSBs (Paiano et al., 2021; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RPA ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The association of RPA with chromatin was strand specific around the DSBs.
source: Moreover, the association of RPA with chromatin was strand specific around the DSBs, consistent with the 5'–3' nature of DNA end resection which generates 3' ssDNA overhangs (Paiano et al., 2021; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RPA ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Extensive DNA end resection was detected in G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells at 4 and 8 hr after AsiSI DSB induction.
source: Using END-seq, we detected extensive DNA end resection in G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells at 4 and 8 hr after AsiSI DSB induction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by END-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In G0-arrested cells, DNA ends are resected at DSBs induced by IR or site-specific endonucleases, generating ssDNA that is bound by RPA.
source: Together, these data indicate that in G0-arrested cells, DNA ends are resected at DSBs induced by IR or site-specific endonucleases, generating ssDNA that is bound by RPA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population correspond to genes encoding proteins that normally promote DNA end resection.
source: gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population correspond to genes encoding proteins that normally promote DNA end resection, while gRNAs enriched in the high RPA population correspond to genes encoding proteins that normally impair resection.
evidence: This is the logic of the CRISPR screen design.

claim: gRNAs enriched in the high RPA population correspond to genes encoding proteins that normally impair resection.
source: gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population correspond to genes encoding proteins that normally promote DNA end resection, while gRNAs enriched in the high RPA population correspond to genes encoding proteins that normally impair resection.
evidence: This is the logic of the CRISPR screen design.

claim: Several gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population target Rbbp8 which encodes the nuclease CtIP.
source: In this screen, we identified several gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population to Rbbp8 which encodes the nuclease CtIP, and Nbn, which encodes the NBN subunit of the MRE11-RAD50-NBN (MRN) complex, consistent with their established roles in promoting DNA end resection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Several gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population target Nbn, which encodes the NBN subunit of the MRE11-RAD50-NBN (MRN) complex.
source: In this screen, we identified several gRNAs enriched in the low RPA staining population to Rbbp8 which encodes the nuclease CtIP, and Nbn, which encodes the NBN subunit of the MRE11-RAD50-NBN (MRN) complex, consistent with their established roles in promoting DNA end resection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: gRNAs targeting Xrcc6 (the gene encoding KU70) were highly enriched in the low RPA population.
source: Unexpectedly, we also found gRNAs targeting Xrcc6 (the gene encoding KU70), Xrcc5 (the gene encoding KU80), and Prkdc (the gene encoding DNA-PKcs) highly enriched in our low RPA population (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: gRNAs targeting Xrcc5 (the gene encoding KU80) were highly enriched in the low RPA population.
source: Unexpectedly, we also found gRNAs targeting Xrcc6 (the gene encoding KU70), Xrcc5 (the gene encoding KU80), and Prkdc (the gene encoding DNA-PKcs) highly enriched in our low RPA population (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: gRNAs targeting Prkdc (the gene encoding DNA-PKcs) were highly enriched in the low RPA population.
source: Unexpectedly, we also found gRNAs targeting Xrcc6 (the gene encoding KU70), Xrcc5 (the gene encoding KU80), and Prkdc (the gene encoding DNA-PKcs) highly enriched in our low RPA population (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DNA-PK may promote DNA end resection in G0 cells.
source: This suggested that DNA-PK may promote DNA end resection in G0 cells, contrary to the established role of these factors in preventing DNA end resection in other phases of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR screen results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Prkdc-/- abl pre-B cells had lower levels of chromatin-bound RPA after IR compared to Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Prkdc-/- abl pre-B cells had lower levels of chromatin-bound RPA after IR compared to Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ATM inhibition did not have a detectable effect on the levels of IR-induced binding of RPA in G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: In contrast to the consistent reduction in the levels of chromatin-bound RPA observed in G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells treated with DNA-PK inhibitor, ATM inhibition did not have a detectable effect on the levels of IR-induced binding of RPA in G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DNA-PK inhibition in wild type abl pre-B cells arrested in G0 showed a modest effect in reducing levels of chromatin-bound RPA.
source: Additionally, DNA-PK inhibition in wild type abl pre-B cells arrested in G0 showed a modest effect in reducing levels of chromatin-bound RPA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A reduced number of IR-induced RPA foci was observed in G0-arrested human MCF10A cells upon inhibition of DNA-PK.
source: The role of DNA-PK in promoting DNA end resection in G0 is not limited to murine abl pre-B cells as we also observed a reduced number of IR-induced RPA foci in G0-arrested human MCF10A cells upon inhibition of DNA-PK (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DNA-PKcs activity, but not ATM, uniquely promotes resection and RPA binding to damaged chromatin after IR in G0 cells.
source: These results indicate that DNA-PKcs activity, but not ATM, uniquely promotes resection and RPA binding to damaged chromatin after IR in G0 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, 1C, 1D.

claim: DNA-PK inhibitor-treated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells showed greatly reduced END-Seq signals distal to DSBs.
source: Consistent with our RPA flow cytometric assay results, DNA-PK inhibitor-treated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells showed greatly reduced END-Seq signals distal to DSBs, consistent with limited DNA end processing when DNA-PK is inactivated (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by END-seq data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DNA-PK activity promotes DNA end resection of DSBs in G0 mammalian cells.
source: These results demonstrate that DNA-PK activity promotes DNA end resection of DSBs in G0 mammalian cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The level of chromatin-bound RPA after IR was greatly reduced in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Xrcc6-/- abl pre-B cells compared to Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: Consistent with our observations in DNA-PK inhibitor-treated G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells and Lig4-/-:Prkdc-/- abl pre-B cells, the level of chromatin-bound RPA after IR was greatly reduced in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Xrcc6-/- abl pre-B cells compared to Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The entire DNA-PK complex is required for DNA end resection in G0 cells.
source: As such, the entire DNA-PK complex is required for DNA end resection in G0 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that both DNA-PKcs and KU70 are required for resection in G0.

claim: gRNAs targeting Fbxl12 were highly enriched in the high RPA staining cell population.
source: In agreement, gRNAs targeting Fbxl12, which encodes the substrate recognition subunit FBXL12 of the SCFFbxl12 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, were highly enriched in our screen in the high RPA staining cell population (Figure 2B), consistent with the idea that the persistent presence of KU70/KU80 at DSBs in cells lacking FBXL12 would lead to extensive DNA end resection.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Fbxl12-/- murine abl pre-B cells, the level of IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA increased compared to Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells.
source: Indeed, we observed that in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Fbxl12-/- murine abl pre-B cells, the level of IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA increased compared to Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Inhibition of DNA-PK with NU7441 in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Fbxl12-/- abl pre-B cells prevented excessive accumulation of RPA on chromatin after IR.
source: Indeed, inhibition of DNA-PK with NU7441 (Figure 3C) and depletion of KU70 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Fbxl12-/- abl pre-B cells prevented excessive accumulation of RPA on chromatin after IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Depletion of KU70 in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Fbxl12-/- abl pre-B cells prevented excessive accumulation of RPA on chromatin after IR.
source: Indeed, inhibition of DNA-PK with NU7441 (Figure 3C) and depletion of KU70 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) in G0-arrested Lig4-/-:Fbxl12-/- abl pre-B cells prevented excessive accumulation of RPA on chromatin after IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ability of DNA-PK to promote DNA end resection in G0 cells is regulated through maintaining proper levels of KU70/KU80 at DNA DSBs by the SCFFbxl12 E3 ubiquitylation complex.
source: Our results suggest that the ability of DNA-PK to promote DNA end resection in G0 cells is regulated through maintaining proper levels of KU70/KU80 at DNA DSBs by the SCFFbxl12 E3 ubiquitylation complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figures 3B, 3C, and 3D.

claim: KU70/KU80 have been shown to prevent DNA end resection in G1 and G2 phases in budding yeast.
source: KU70/KU80 have been shown to prevent DNA end resection in G1 and G2 phases in budding yeast and in S phase in mammalian cells but has not been examined in G0 cells (Lee et al., 1998; Clerici et al., 2008; Shao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lee et al., 1998; Clerici et al., 2008; Shao et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of DNA-PKcs (Lig4-/-:Prkdc-/-) did not reduce the levels of IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA in G2-arrested or cycling G1 phase cells.
source: In contrast to G0 cells, loss of DNA-PKcs (Lig4-/-:Prkdc-/-) did not reduce the levels of IR-induced chromatin-bound RPA in G2-arrested or cycling G1 phase cells (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Similar results were obtained when analyzing Lig4-/-:Xrcc6-/- abl pre-B cells in G2-arrested or cycling G1 phase.
source: Similar results were obtained when analyzing Lig4-/-:Xrcc6-/- abl pre-B cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells treated with DNA-PK inhibitor exhibited significantly reduced END-seq signals in regions distal to the DSBs.
source: Whereas G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells treated with DNA-PK inhibitor exhibited significantly reduced END-seq signals in regions distal to the DSBs, the same treatment had little effect in cells arrested in G2 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by END-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DNA-PK inhibitor treatment had little effect on END-seq signals in cells arrested in G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Whereas G0-arrested Lig4-/- abl pre-B cells treated with DNA-PK inhibitor exhibited significantly reduced END-seq signals in regions distal to the DSBs, the same treatment had little effect in cells arrested in G2 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by END-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Resection tract lengths were on average 3–4 kb in the G0-arrested cells and were greatly reduced upon treatment with DNA-PK inhibitor.
source: Quantitation of the resection tract lengths from the End-seq analysis showed that they were on average 3–4 kb in the G0-arrested cells and were greatly reduced upon treatment with DNA-PK inhibitor (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of END-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The resection tract lengths in G2 arrested cells were minimally affected by treatment with DNA-PK inhibitor.
source: In comparison, the resection tract lengths in G2 arrested cells were minimally affected by treatment with DNA-PK inhibitor (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of END-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NHEJ-proficient wild-type MCF10A cells arrested in G0, but not cells in G1 phase, exhibited reduced RPA on chromatin after IR upon DNA-PK inhibition.
source: Additionally, NHEJ-proficient wild-type MCF10A cells arrested in G0, but not cells in G1 phase, exhibited reduced RPA on chromatin after IR upon DNA-PK inhibition (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DNA-PK distinctly promotes DNA end resection at DSBs in mammalian cells in G0 but not in other cell cycle phases.
source: These results suggest that DNA-PK distinctly promotes DNA end resection at DSBs in mammalian cells in G0 but not in other cell cycle phases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 4.

claim: DNA end resection dependent on CtIP and MRE11 occurs at DSBs in G0 mammalian cells.
source: However, in this study we revealed that DNA end resection dependent on CtIP and MRE11, which are required for resection in S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, occurs at DSBs in G0 mammalian cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CtIP activity in G1, G2 and S phases requires its phosphorylation.
source: Because CtIP activity in G1, G2 and S phases requires its phosphorylation, this is likely to be the case in G0 cells and future studies will identify the kinase responsible for any CtIP phosphorylation in G0 cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: CtIP activity in G0 cells likely requires its phosphorylation.
source: Because CtIP activity in G1, G2 and S phases requires its phosphorylation, this is likely to be the case in G0 cells and future studies will identify the kinase responsible for any CtIP phosphorylation in G0 cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known requirement for CtIP phosphorylation in other cell cycle phases.

claim: The kinase activity of DNA-PK is critical for resection of DSBs in G0 cells.
source: In addition to CtIP and MRE11, we identified additional factors that promote resection in G0 cells as components of the DNA-PK complex, including KU70, KU80, and DNA-PKcs, in a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen and showed that the kinase activity of DNA-PK is critical as resection of DSBs diminishes upon DNA-PK inhibitor treatment (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Loss of FBXL12 results in aberrant accumulation of KU70/KU80 at DSBs.
source: As the SCFFBXL12 E3 ubiquitin is thought to limit the abundance of the KU70/KU80 heterodimer (Postow and Funabiki, 2013), our data are in line with the notion that loss of FBXL12 results in aberrant accumulation of KU70/KU80 at DSBs, and consequently elevated or prolonged activation of DNA-PK at DSBs which promotes resection in G0 cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about FBXL12 function and the experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: Loss of FBXL12 results in elevated or prolonged activation of DNA-PK at DSBs which promotes resection in G0 cells.
source: As the SCFFBXL12 E3 ubiquitin is thought to limit the abundance of the KU70/KU80 heterodimer (Postow and Funabiki, 2013), our data are in line with the notion that loss of FBXL12 results in aberrant accumulation of KU70/KU80 at DSBs, and consequently elevated or prolonged activation of DNA-PK at DSBs which promotes resection in G0 cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: Chemical modifications or secondary structures at DSBs have been identified as requiring DNA end processing to create a more accessible repair environment.
source: Chemical modifications or secondary structures at DSBs have been identified as requiring DNA end processing to create a more accessible repair environment, which could presumably be the case at DSBs in G0 cells (Weinfeld and Soderlind, 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Weinfeld and Soderlind, 1991.

claim: Artemis is an endo and exonuclease which is activated by DNA-PKcs.
source: For example, Artemis is an endo and exonuclease which is activated by DNA-PKcs and uses its nuclease activity to open DNA hairpins at coding ends, which is required for V(D)J recombination, and cleaves 3' ssDNA overhangs during NHEJ (Ma et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ma et al., 2002 and Ma et al., 2005.

claim: Artemis uses its nuclease activity to open DNA hairpins at coding ends, which is required for V(D)J recombination.
source: For example, Artemis is an endo and exonuclease which is activated by DNA-PKcs and uses its nuclease activity to open DNA hairpins at coding ends, which is required for V(D)J recombination, and cleaves 3' ssDNA overhangs during NHEJ (Ma et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ma et al., 2002 and Ma et al., 2005.

claim: Artemis cleaves 3' ssDNA overhangs during NHEJ.
source: For example, Artemis is an endo and exonuclease which is activated by DNA-PKcs and uses its nuclease activity to open DNA hairpins at coding ends, which is required for V(D)J recombination, and cleaves 3' ssDNA overhangs during NHEJ (Ma et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ma et al., 2002 and Ma et al., 2005.

claim: Artemis was shown to contribute to slow, resection dependent NHEJ repair in G1 phase cells.
source: Artemis was also recently shown to contribute to slow, resection dependent NHEJ repair in G1 phase cells (Biehs et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Biehs et al., 2017.

claim: DNA end resection in G0 may result in substrates that are ideal for Pol Theta-mediated end joining (TMEJ).
source: It is additionally possible that DNA end resection in G0 results in substrates that are ideal for Pol Theta-mediated end joining (TMEJ).
evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of resection in G0 cells.

claim: TMEJ occurs after extensive DNA end resection when HR is not possible or when substrates are not suitable for NHEJ.
source: TMEJ occurs after extensive DNA end resection when HR is not possible or when substrates are not suitable for NHEJ, which could be the case at a subset of breaks in G0 (Yousefzadeh et al., 2014; Wyatt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Yousefzadeh et al., 2014 and Wyatt et al., 2016.

claim: TMEJ is KU70/KU80 independent.
source: However, it is notably that TMEJ is KU70/KU80 independent, while the resection that we see in G0 is KU70/KU80 dependent.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: The resection observed in G0 is KU70/KU80 dependent.
source: However, it is notably that TMEJ is KU70/KU80 independent, while the resection that we see in G0 is KU70/KU80 dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DNA end resection has a role in recruiting anti-resection factors to limit extensive DNA end resection.
source: Interestingly, DNA end resection has a role in recruiting anti-resection factors to limit extensive DNA end resection.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: The SHLD2 component of Shieldin binds ssDNA, suppresses RAD51 loading, and ultimately limits DNA end resection by preventing access to resection nucleases.
source: The SHLD2 component of Shieldin binds ssDNA, suppresses RAD51 loading, and ultimately limits DNA end resection by preventing access to resection nucleases (Noordermeer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Noordermeer et al., 2018.

claim: HELB is a 5'–3' DNA helicase that binds to RPA and limits EXO1 and BLM-DNA2-mediated DNA end resection.
source: HELB, a 5'–3' DNA helicase, binds to RPA and limits EXO1 and BLM-DNA2-mediated DNA end resection (Tkáč et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tkáč et al., 2016.

claim: Limited DNA end resection in G0 cells could be important in preventing more extensive DNA end resection.
source: In this way, limited DNA end resection in G0 cells could be important in preventing more extensive DNA end resection.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of limited resection in G0 cells.

claim: DNA end resection in G0 cells is likely not resulting in aberrant HR but may be required to create more accessible DNA ends and/or to recruit anti-resection factors.
source: Altogether, we propose that DNA end resection in G0 cells is likely not resulting in aberrant HR but may be required to create more accessible DNA ends and/or to recruit anti-resection factors.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of resection in G0 cells.

claim: At HO endonuclease breaks in budding yeast, deletion of KU70/KU80 leads to ssDNA accumulation in G1 cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: For example, at HO endonuclease breaks in budding yeast, deletion of KU70/KU80 leads to ssDNA accumulation in G1 cells and increased MRE11 recruitment to DSBs compared to wild-type cells (Lee et al., 1998; Clerici et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lee et al., 1998 and Clerici et al., 2008.

claim: At HO endonuclease breaks in budding yeast, deletion of KU70/KU80 leads to increased MRE11 recruitment to DSBs compared to wild-type cells.
source: For example, at HO endonuclease breaks in budding yeast, deletion of KU70/KU80 leads to ssDNA accumulation in G1 cells and increased MRE11 recruitment to DSBs compared to wild-type cells (Lee et al., 1998; Clerici et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lee et al., 1998 and Clerici et al., 2008.

claim: In budding yeast, at inducible I-SceI DSBs, deletion of KU70 results in increased RFA1 foci formation in G1.
source: Also in budding yeast, at inducible I-SceI DSBs, deletion of KU70 results in increased RFA1 foci formation in G1, but deletion of NHEJ factor DNA Ligase IV leads to no defect in RFA1 foci formation compared to wild-type cells, indicating that KU70 itself, not NHEJ, is a barrier to DNA end resection (Barlow et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Barlow et al., 2008.

claim: In budding yeast, deletion of NHEJ factor DNA Ligase IV leads to no defect in RFA1 foci formation compared to wild-type cells.
source: Also in budding yeast, at inducible I-SceI DSBs, deletion of KU70 results in increased RFA1 foci formation in G1, but deletion of NHEJ factor DNA Ligase IV leads to no defect in RFA1 foci formation compared to wild-type cells, indicating that KU70 itself, not NHEJ, is a barrier to DNA end resection (Barlow et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Barlow et al., 2008.

claim: In budding yeast, KU70 itself, not NHEJ, is a barrier to DNA end resection.
source: Also in budding yeast, at inducible I-SceI DSBs, deletion of KU70 results in increased RFA1 foci formation in G1, but deletion of NHEJ factor DNA Ligase IV leads to no defect in RFA1 foci formation compared to wild-type cells, indicating that KU70 itself, not NHEJ, is a barrier to DNA end resection (Barlow et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results cited from Barlow et al., 2008.

claim: In mammalian cells, complementation of KU70/KU80 knockout cells with a M. tuberculosis KU homolog persistently bound to DSBs in S phase results in reduced RPA and RAD51 foci formation after IR.
source: In mammalian cells, complementation of KU70/KU80 knockout cells with a M. tuberculosis KU homolog persistently bound to DSBs in S phase results in reduced RPA and RAD51 foci formation after IR (Shao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Shao et al., 2012.

claim: In G0 cells, KU70/KU80 promotes DNA end resection.
source: Contrary to these roles for KU70/KU80 in protecting DNA ends from nucleolytic attack, we found that in G0 cells, KU70/KU80 promotes DNA end resection (Figures 3A and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 4B.

claim: KU70/KU80 promotes resection through recruitment and activation of DNA-PKcs at DSBs.
source: We hypothesize that KU70/KU80 promotes resection through recruitment and activation of DNA-PKcs at DSBs (Gottlieb and Jackson, 1993), as we also found that DNA-PKcs inhibition and genetic deletion of Prkdc leads to less RPA on chromatin after IR and shorter tracts of DNA end resection in G0 cells (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D, 4A, 4C, 4D).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data and established knowledge about DNA-PK complex formation.

claim: Most studies establishing the role of KU70/KU80 in protecting DNA ends were performed in S. cerevisiae which do not have a homolog to DNA-PKcs.
source: It is important to note that most studies establishing the role of KU70/KU80 in protecting DNA ends were performed in S. cerevisiae which do not have a homolog to DNA-PKcs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: The function of DNA-PK promoting DNA end resection in G0 cells may not be evolutionarily conserved.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the function of DNA-PK promoting DNA end resection in G0 cells may not be evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that S. cerevisiae lacks DNA-PKcs.

claim: Previous studies in S. cerevisiae and mammalian cells establishing DNA-PK as a pro-NHEJ complex did not analyze G0 cells.
source: Moreover, previous studies in S. cerevisiae and mammalian cells establishing DNA-PK as a pro-NHEJ complex did not analyze G0 cells.
evidence: This is an observation about the literature in the field.

claim: DNA-PK does not promote DNA end resection in G1 or G2 phase cells.
source: We found that DNA-PK does not promote DNA end resection in G1 or G2 phase cells, only in G0-arrested cells, indicating that DNA-PK-dependent DNA end resection is unique to G0, but is not contradictory to its anti-resection function in G1 or G2 phase cells (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In G0 cells, KU70/KU80 could protect some DNA ends, but after recruitment and activation of DNA-PKcs, the net effect is DNA end resection.
source: In G0 cells, KU70/KU80 could protect some DNA ends, but after recruitment and activation of DNA-PKcs, the net effect is DNA end resection.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of DNA-PK function in G0 cells.

claim: ATM and DNA-PK have been shown to have some overlapping functions in DNA damage response and repair, including phosphorylation of H2A.X in response to IR.
source: ATM and DNA-PK have been shown to have some overlapping functions in DNA damage response and repair, including phosphorylation of H2A.X in response to IR and signal join formation during V(D)J recombination (Stiff et al., 2004; Gapud et al., 2011; Zha et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Stiff et al., 2004; Gapud et al., 2011; Zha et al., 2011.

claim: ATM and DNA-PK have been shown to have some overlapping functions in signal join formation during V(D)J recombination.
source: ATM and DNA-PK have been shown to have some overlapping functions in DNA damage response and repair, including phosphorylation of H2A.X in response to IR and signal join formation during V(D)J recombination (Stiff et al., 2004; Gapud et al., 2011; Zha et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Stiff et al., 2004; Gapud et al., 2011; Zha et al., 2011.

claim: DNA-PK promotes resection in G0 cells, but ATM does not have a detectable impact.
source: However, we find that this is not the case during DNA end resection in G0 cells as DNA-PK promotes resection in G0 cells, but ATM does not have a detectable impact (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ATM has been implicated in promoting HR repair by phosphorylating CtIP and promoting KU70/KU80 removal from DSBs.
source: ATM has been implicated in promoting HR repair by phosphorylating CtIP and promoting KU70/KU80 removal from DSBs, as well as phosphorylating DNA-PKcs at single-ended DSBs to remove it from these breaks that require DNA end resection (Wang et al., 2013; Britton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Wang et al., 2013 and Britton et al., 2020.

claim: ATM has been implicated in phosphorylating DNA-PKcs at single-ended DSBs to remove it from these breaks that require DNA end resection.
source: ATM has been implicated in promoting HR repair by phosphorylating CtIP and promoting KU70/KU80 removal from DSBs, as well as phosphorylating DNA-PKcs at single-ended DSBs to remove it from these breaks that require DNA end resection (Wang et al., 2013; Britton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Wang et al., 2013 and Britton et al., 2020.

claim: DNA-PKcs autophosphorylation promotes HR by removing it from DSBs to allow nuclease access.
source: DNA-PKcs autophosphorylation promotes HR by removing it from DSBs to allow nuclease access but is typically associated with promoting NHEJ by phosphorylating Artemis, XRCC4, and XLF (Zhou and Paull, 2013; Bartlett and Lees-Miller, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Zhou and Paull, 2013 and Bartlett and Lees-Miller, 2018.

claim: DNA-PKcs autophosphorylation is typically associated with promoting NHEJ by phosphorylating Artemis, XRCC4, and XLF.
source: DNA-PKcs autophosphorylation promotes HR by removing it from DSBs to allow nuclease access but is typically associated with promoting NHEJ by phosphorylating Artemis, XRCC4, and XLF (Zhou and Paull, 2013; Bartlett and Lees-Miller, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Zhou and Paull, 2013 and Bartlett and Lees-Miller, 2018.

claim: DNA-PKcs could be acting in place of ATM to promote DNA end resection in G0 cells.
source: So while ATM often promotes DNA end resection and HR, it appears that DNA-PKcs could be acting in place of ATM to promote DNA end resection in G0 cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: DNA-PKcs may phosphorylate a unique substrate(s) in G0 cells that promotes DNA end resection.
source: It is additionally possible that DNA-PKcs phosphorylates a unique substrate(s) in G0 cells that promotes DNA end resection.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of DNA-PKcs function in G0 cells.

claim: Some aspects of DSB repair in G0 function differently than DSB repair in cycling cells.
source: In summary, we provide here evidence that DNA-PK promotes DNA end resection uniquely in G0 cells, and that this DNA end resection is counteracted by FBXL12. We speculate that some aspects of DSB repair in G0 function differently than DSB repair in cycling cells, and future studies may reveal the mechanism and utility of these key differences.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The majority of AsiSI DSBs are within 2 kb of the transcriptional start site of transcriptionally active genes.
source: To determine the extent of DNA end processing in G0 cells, we performed END-seq (Canela et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2021) to directly measure DNA end resection at nucleotide resolution at AsiSI-induced DSBs, the majority of which are within 2 kb of the transcriptional start site of transcriptionally active genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
